title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why is a model's willingness to argue any position without believing it an asset in this module and a liability elsewhere?
options: Because rehearsal doesn't require factual accuracy, so hallucination is harmless here
Because you need a sparring partner with no stake and no social reason to go easy — the same indifference that makes fluent output untrustworthy makes attack honest
Because models argue better than they explain
It isn't an asset — the module works despite this property, not because of it
questions.explanation: Elsewhere, arguing convincingly without belief is exactly why output needs verification. Here it's the point: no colleague will attack your plan with that little social friction. A overstates it: accuracy still matters, which is why Lesson 4 traces wrong objections.

questions.prompt: You ask a model "what do you think of this plan?" and get praise, three considerations, and a balanced close. What happened?
options: The plan is genuinely strong and the model found little to object to
The model's critical capabilities are weaker than its generative ones
You asked for the wrong thing — the plausible continuation of that question is a constructive-colleague response, which reads as critique and functions as endorsement
The context window was too short to support a thorough critique
questions.explanation: Nothing malfunctioned. The mechanism is 101's: most plausible continuation. The failure is dangerous precisely because it feels like having been reviewed.

questions.prompt: Which instruction is most likely to produce usable objections?
options: "Be critical of this plan and don't hold back"
"You manage a team of nine with operating targets and you have to defend this on Monday — what questions can't you answer?"
"List the pros and cons of this approach"
"Rate this plan out of ten and explain the score"
questions.explanation: A role with an interest and something at stake. A produces criticism-flavoured text because "critical" is a style instruction, not a position. C invites the balanced close the module is trying to defeat.

questions.prompt: What does the fourth adversary (the person with the least power affected) exist to surface?
options: Legal exposure from the most vulnerable group
What you normalized, from the perspective of someone structurally absent from the room where the plan was built
The strongest emotional reaction, for communications planning
Whether the change is defensible under 101 M7's line
questions.explanation: They're in the set because representing that person is structurally an HRBP's job and they are almost never in the design conversation. A and D are things this adversary may incidentally surface; the purpose is the blind spot.

questions.prompt: Which single prompt does the module identify as the highest-yield?
options: "What's the strongest objection to this?"
"What would the headline say if this went badly?"
"What am I not asking you because I don't want to know the answer?"
"Are you sure about that objection?"
questions.explanation: It targets what your own preparation is structurally blind to. You can't audit your omissions from inside them. D is the module's named non-move: self-confirmation isn't verification here any more than it was in 101 M6.

questions.prompt: Why should the rehearsal happen in a fresh conversation rather than the one where you built the plan?
options: Long conversations exceed the context window and drop the plan
The building conversation contains all your justifications, and the model predicts from everything in view — so it argues from inside your framing
Models perform better on the first exchange of any conversation
Fresh conversations are cheaper in token terms
questions.explanation: 101 M1's mechanism. Give it the plan and the role, not the story of how you arrived at the plan, otherwise you've briefed your adversary with your own defence.

questions.prompt: An adversary raises an objection that rests on a false assumption about your organization. The practitioner move is to:
options: Dismiss it and move on — the objection is invalid
Correct the model and re-run the adversary with better context
Ask how it got there — because a false inference drawn from your written plan is a communication defect a human reader would make faster
Accept it anyway, since the perception matters more than the fact
questions.explanation: The wrong objection is still evidence about how the plan reads without your context. B isn't wrong as a follow-up, but it skips the free finding. D over-corrects into treating every misreading as valid.

questions.prompt: What is the module's own claim against itself?
options: That adversarial rehearsal is less effective than rehearsing with a human colleague
That preparation and confidence move independently, and a rehearsal can deliver only the second — generating counters for every objection while the plan stays unchanged
That the technique only works for high-stakes conversations
That models are too agreeable for the technique to work reliably
questions.explanation: Rationalization wearing rehearsal's clothes, and it feels identical from the inside, which is why the activity weights "what did you change?" most heavily. D is the problem Lesson 3 solves, not the residual risk the claim names.
